title: How Sleepwalking Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore sleepwalking (somnambulism): the 1845 Weymouth, Massachusetts murder of prostitute Maria Anne Bickford by Albert Terrell, who was acquitted on a sleepwalking defense; the official definition and symptoms; when it occurs in non-REM deep sleep; whether to wake a sleepwalker; that it usually happens once per night and lasts seconds to half an hour; that it runs in families, is more common in children and identical twins, and can signal Parkinson's, Alzheimer's or stress; sleep deprivation and noise as triggers; other parasomnias including sleep sex and sleep eating linked to the drug Ambien, including a sleep-emailing case; a sleepwalker who fell from a hotel room in Majorca and a man who sleepwalked into quicksand on Holy Island; the hosts' personal sleepwalking anecdotes; REM sleep behavior disorder; and a listener mail story about a grandmother's marijuana garden.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor tease
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, with a brief sponsor line at the start and banter before the topic begins.

segments.title: 1845 Weymouth murder and sleepwalking defense
segments.summary: Josh recounts the murder of Maria Anne Bickford in Weymouth, Massachusetts, by her wealthy boyfriend Albert Terrell, who claimed he was sleepwalking and was acquitted despite setting fires in the brothel. They note the jury's biases and the limited understanding of sleepwalking at the time, and mention a recent Illinois acquittal.

segments.title: Definition and timing of sleepwalking
segments.summary: The hosts give the official definition of sleepwalking (somnambulism) from the DSM-IV, its symptoms and impact on life, and explain it occurs in non-REM deep sleep when the body moves but the brain is largely off.

segments.title: Waking a sleepwalker and typical episodes
segments.summary: Discussion of whether it is dangerous to wake a sleepwalker, advice to guide them gently back to bed, the fact that most people sleepwalk only once a night for thirty seconds to half an hour, and what sleepwalkers can do while asleep.

segments.title: Genetics, age, and causes
segments.summary: Sleepwalking runs in families, is far more common in children and identical twins, and adults who start for the first time should be checked for conditions like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's. Stress has been linked to it. Competing theories include sleep deprivation, noise triggers, arousal between sleep and wake, and hormones in children.

segments.title: Sleepwalking crimes and injuries
segments.summary: The hosts discuss people who have killed or assaulted others while sleepwalking with mixed court outcomes, and a survey finding eleven percent of sleepwalkers reported injuries.

segments.title: Other parasomnias: sleep sex, sleep eating, sleep emailing
segments.summary: Overview of other parasomnias including sleep sex, and sleep eating linked to the drug Ambien, with the case of a woman who sent odd emails while asleep. A sleepwalker's hotel fall in Majorca and a Holy Island quicksand incident are also described.

segments.title: Personal sleepwalking and sleep talking stories
segments.summary: Josh recounts his uncle's sleepwalking incidents and Chuck describes his own sleepwalking and sleep talking, and a discussion of REM sleep behavior disorder, where people act out dreams.

segments.title: Listener mail: pot-growing grandmother
segments.summary: A listener named KM shares a story about a grandmother who grew marijuana in her Pennsylvania yard, with seeds obtained through a college friend.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send in stories and points to the website for more on sleepwalking, then signs off with a sponsor line.
